concepts.name: Tripitaka: Structure and Tripartite Division
key_dimensions: Three constituent Pitakas — Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma — and their distinct domains
UPSC trap: distinguishing which Pitaka contains doctrinal philosophy vs. monastic rules vs. discourses
Collective meaning of 'Pitaka' (basket) and oral-to-written transmission history
Comparison with Jain canonical literature (Agamas) to highlight structural differences

concepts.name: Vinaya Pitaka: Monastic Code and Its Sub-divisions
key_dimensions: Three sub-sections: Suttavibhanga, Khandhaka, and Parivara — their specific content
Role in regulating Sangha discipline: rules for monks (Bhikkhus) and nuns (Bhikkhunis)
UPSC trap: Vinaya Pitaka is NOT a source of Buddhist philosophy — it is administrative/legal in nature
Historical significance as evidence for early Buddhist monastic organization and gender inclusion

concepts.name: Sutta Pitaka: Discourses of the Buddha and Its Five Nikayas
key_dimensions: Five Nikayas: Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, Anguttara, Khuddaka — length and thematic classification
UPSC trap: Khuddaka Nikaya is the largest and most diverse, containing the Dhammapada and Jataka tales
Sutta Pitaka as the primary source for Buddha's ethical and philosophical teachings
Distinction between Sutta Pitaka (Pali Canon) and Sanskrit Sutra literature of Mahayana Buddhism

concepts.name: Abhidhamma Pitaka: Higher Philosophy and Scholastic Analysis
key_dimensions: Seven books of the Abhidhamma and their focus on systematic psychological/metaphysical analysis
UPSC trap: Abhidhamma is considered a later addition — its authorship is debated (not directly attributed to Buddha)
Distinction from Sutta Pitaka: Abhidhamma replaces narrative with abstract scholastic categorization
Theravada vs. Sarvastivada versions of Abhidhamma — doctrinal divergence across schools

concepts.name: Pali Language and the Theravada Canon
key_dimensions: Pali as the liturgical language of Theravada Buddhism — its relationship to Magadhi Prakrit
UPSC trap: Sanskrit was used for Mahayana texts, NOT for the original Tripitaka (which is in Pali)
Geographic spread: Pali Canon preserved in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand — implications for transmission
Significance of Pali as a historical source for reconstructing Mauryan-era social and economic life

concepts.name: Buddhist Councils and Codification of the Tripitaka
key_dimensions: Four major Buddhist Councils: location, patron, president, and outcome for canonical texts
UPSC trap: First Council (Rajagriha) — Vinaya recited by Upali, Dhamma by Ananda — not yet written down
Third Council (Pataliputra, under Ashoka) — addition of Abhidhamma Pitaka and dispatch of missionaries
Fourth Council: Two versions — Theravada (Sri Lanka, 1st century BCE) vs. Sarvastivada (Kashmir, Kanishka) — UPSC frequently tests this duality

concepts.name: Dhammapada: Content, Significance, and Placement
key_dimensions: Part of Khuddaka Nikaya within the Sutta Pitaka — 423 verses on ethical conduct
UPSC trap: Dhammapada is NOT a separate text outside the Tripitaka — it belongs within the Khuddaka Nikaya
Dhammapada as the most widely translated Buddhist text — its role in popular Buddhist ethics
Comparison with Upanishadic thought: shared themes of mind, karma, and the path to liberation

concepts.name: Jataka Tales: Classification, Purpose, and Historical Value
key_dimensions: 547 Jataka stories in the Khuddaka Nikaya — depicting Buddha's previous lives (Bodhisattva concept)
UPSC trap: Jataka tales are a source for social and economic history (guilds, trade, occupations) of 6th–3rd century BCE
Artistic representation: Jataka scenes at Sanchi, Bharhut, Ajanta — linking literature to archaeology
Distinction: Jatakas are canonical (Theravada) vs. non-canonical Avadana literature of Mahayana tradition

concepts.name: Milindapanha: Nature, Authorship, and Canonical Status
key_dimensions: A dialogue between King Menander (Milinda) and monk Nagasena — Indo-Greek philosophical exchange
UPSC trap: Milindapanha is NOT part of the Tripitaka — it is a para-canonical text, included only in the Burmese Pali Canon
Historical significance as evidence for Indo-Greek interactions and spread of Buddhism in Northwest India
Key philosophical themes: nature of the self (Anatman), rebirth without a soul — doctrinal nuances tested by UPSC

concepts.name: Theravada vs. Mahayana Buddhist Literature: Canonical Divergence
key_dimensions: Theravada canon = Pali Tripitaka; Mahayana canon includes Sanskrit Sutras (Prajnaparamita, Lotus Sutra, etc.)
UPSC trap: Mahayana texts are NOT part of the Tripitaka — they represent a separate and later literary tradition
Concept of Buddhavacana (word of the Buddha) — debate over what qualifies as authentic Buddhist scripture
Vajrayana Tantric texts as a third layer — entirely outside the Tripitaka framework

concepts.name: Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa: Chronicles vs. Canonical Texts
key_dimensions: Sri Lankan Pali chronicles — Dipavamsa (4th century CE) and Mahavamsa (5th century CE) — historical narratives
UPSC trap: These are NOT part of the Tripitaka — they are historical chronicles (Vamsas), not canonical texts
Significance for reconstructing Ashokan history, spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and Buddhist kingship ideology
Mahavamsa's account of the Third Buddhist Council — corroborating and contradicting other sources

concepts.name: Buddhaghosa and Visuddhimagga: Post-Canonical Commentary Tradition
key_dimensions: Buddhaghosa (5th century CE) — most important Theravada commentator, authored Visuddhimagga (Path of Purification)
UPSC trap: Visuddhimagga is a commentary (Atthakatha), NOT part of the original Tripitaka
Role of Pali commentaries in standardizing Theravada doctrine — distinction between canonical and post-canonical authority
Buddhaghosa's work as evidence for the flourishing of Buddhist scholarship in Sri Lanka under Sinhalese patronage

concepts.name: Oral Transmission and Writing of the Tripitaka
key_dimensions: Tripitaka preserved orally for ~400 years before being written down at the Fourth Council in Sri Lanka (1st century BCE)
UPSC trap: Ashoka's role was in missionary dispatch and council patronage — he did NOT cause the Tripitaka to be written
Significance of the Bhanakas (reciters) tradition — specialist monks responsible for memorizing specific Pitakas
Writing of Tripitaka on palm leaves in Sri Lanka — implications for textual preservation and variant readings

concepts.name: Tripitaka as a Source for Reconstructing Early Indian History
key_dimensions: Evidence for the Mahajanapada political system, republican polities (Vajji, Malla), and monarchical states
Economic data: trade routes, merchant guilds (Shrenis), currency, and urban centers of the Gangetic plain
UPSC trap: Tripitaka is a religious text but serves as a primary historical source — distinguishing its historical vs. doctrinal utility
Social history: caste practices, position of women, Shudra occupations — corroboration with Jataka tales and Arthashastra

concepts.name: Anguttara Nikaya and the List of Sixteen Mahajanapadas
key_dimensions: Anguttara Nikaya (part of Sutta Pitaka) provides the canonical list of 16 Mahajanapadas
UPSC trap: The Digha Nikaya also lists kingdoms but the authoritative 16-Mahajanapada list is from Anguttara Nikaya
Cross-referencing with Jain text Bhagavati Sutra — slight differences in the list and their historical implications
Geographical reconstruction of 6th century BCE India using Nikaya evidence — limitations of textual geography

concepts.name: Khuddaka Nikaya: Composition, Diversity, and Importance
key_dimensions: 15 (or 18) texts including Dhammapada, Jatakas, Theragatha, Therigatha, Sutta Nipata, Udana — widest thematic range
UPSC trap: Khuddaka Nikaya is the LARGEST Nikaya and also the most heterogeneous — often confused as a minor collection due to its name ('minor')
Therigatha — verses of elder nuns — as evidence for women's participation in early Buddhism and their spiritual equality
Sutta Nipata as one of the oldest texts in the Pali Canon — used to reconstruct proto-Buddhist teachings

concepts.name: Therigatha: Women in Early Buddhism and Literary Significance
key_dimensions: Part of Khuddaka Nikaya — 73 poems by early Buddhist nuns (Theris) — unique gendered perspective in ancient Indian literature
UPSC trap: Therigatha is the ONLY text in the ancient world entirely devoted to women's spiritual experiences — its uniqueness must be noted
Evidence for the existence of the Bhikkhuni Sangha and its tensions with patriarchal Brahmanical society
Historical value: names of nuns, their social backgrounds (courtesans, queens, mothers) — snapshot of women across social strata

concepts.name: Tripitaka and the Concept of Buddhavacana (Word of Buddha)
key_dimensions: Buddhavacana = authoritative utterances of the Buddha — the criterion for inclusion in the canon
UPSC trap: Not all texts in the Tripitaka were directly spoken by Buddha — Vinaya rules were codified by the Sangha, Abhidhamma authorship is debated
Schism between Theravada and Mahayana over what constitutes Buddhavacana — doctrinal authority and canonical boundaries
Implications for understanding how religious authority was constructed and contested in early Buddhist history

concepts.name: Ashoka's Role in Propagating Buddhist Literature
key_dimensions: Ashoka's Rock Edicts and Pillar Edicts refer to specific Dhamma texts — possible references to Tripitaka passages
UPSC trap: Ashoka's Bhabru Edict recommends specific Buddhist texts to monks and nuns — but these are NOT identical to the Tripitaka divisions
Dispatch of Dharma missionaries (Dharmaduta) including Mahinda to Sri Lanka — carrying oral Tripitaka tradition
Controversy: Whether Ashoka patronized Buddhism exclusively or promoted a syncretic Dhamma — implications for reading Pali sources

concepts.name: Tripitaka vs. Jain Agamas: Comparative Canonical Structure
key_dimensions: Jain canon (Agamas/Siddhanta): 12 Angas, 12 Upangas — oral tradition compiled at Councils of Pataliputra and Valabhi
UPSC trap: Both Tripitaka and Agamas suffered from debate over authenticity — Digambara Jains reject the existing Agamas as corrupt
Language contrast: Tripitaka in Pali; Agamas in Ardhamagadhi — both Prakrits but serving distinct sectarian traditions
Thematic overlap: Both address monastic discipline, cosmology, and lay ethics — but differ fundamentally on soul (Atman/Jiva) and liberation
